title: Why is using REQUIRES_NEW + synchronous REST calls to mimic a Saga an anti-pattern, and what is the correct refactor?
shortTitle: Why is REQUIRES_NEW + sync REST calls a Saga anti-pattern?
keyPoints: A pseudo-saga holds a database connection open while making a synchronous HTTP call to another service
REQUIRES_NEW makes it worse by holding two connections per thread during the network wait
Connections are wasted during network latency (2-30 seconds) while the database is idle
Under load this exhausts the connection pool even though the database itself is healthy
Each REQUIRES_NEW commits independently, so earlier commits cannot be undone if a later step fails
The correct refactor is the Transactional Outbox pattern: short DB-only transaction plus async event relay
Real Saga patterns use local transactions per step with compensating actions for rollback

s1_definition.oneliner: Never hold a database connection while waiting on a network call -- REQUIRES_NEW plus synchronous REST calls waste pool connections during network latency and create a distributed monolith disguised as microservices.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Pseudo-saga** -- a pattern where a transactional method holds a database connection open while calling another service over HTTP. The connection is held for the entire network round trip.
- **Connection waste** -- during the 2-30 second REST call, the database connection is checked out but idle. The database has no work to do, but the pool slot is occupied.
- **Double connection problem** -- REQUIRES_NEW suspends the outer connection and opens a second one, so one thread pins two connections during the slow HTTP call.
- **Pool starvation** -- with 20 connections and 3-second partner calls, throughput is capped at roughly 7 requests per second. Beyond that, requests fail with "Connection is not available."
- **Not a real Saga** -- a real Saga uses local transactions per step with compensating actions. The pseudo-saga has no compensation and no atomicity across services.
- **Correct refactor** -- Transactional Outbox: write business data and an outbox event in one short transaction, then relay the event asynchronously via Kafka to the partner service.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a teller holds one vault key (connection) open while calling the partner bank (ICICI) on the phone. The phone call takes 30 seconds. During those 30 seconds, the vault key is wasted -- nobody else can use it. If 20 tellers all call partner banks simultaneously, all 20 keys are tied up on phone calls, and the vault is effectively closed for new customers. The fix: the teller finishes the vault work in 10 milliseconds, puts the key back, and drops a note in an outbox. A separate courier picks up the note and makes the phone call.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Pseudo-Saga (WRONG)                                     │
│                                                          │
│  @Transactional {                                        │
│    debit SAV2001          (10ms DB work)                 │
│    REST call to ICICI     (3000ms network wait)          │
│    commit                 (5ms)                          │
│  }                                                       │
│                                                          │
│  Connection held: ████████████████████████████ 3015ms     │
│  Actual DB work:  █ 15ms                                 │
│  Wasted:          ░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░ 3000ms      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Transactional Outbox (CORRECT)                          │
│                                                          │
│  @Transactional {                                        │
│    debit SAV2001          (10ms)                         │
│    write outbox event     (5ms)                          │
│    commit                 (5ms)                          │
│  }                                                       │
│  Connection held: █ 20ms                                 │
│                                                          │
│  Outbox Relay (separate process):                        │
│    read outbox event                                     │
│    publish to Kafka                                      │
│    mark event PUBLISHED                                  │
│                                                          │
│  Partner Consumer:                                       │
│    receive Kafka event                                   │
│    call ICICI REST API    (3000ms, own connection)        │
│    mark event PROCESSED                                  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The pseudo-saga anti-pattern holds a database connection open while making a synchronous REST call to another service. The connection is wasted during the entire network wait because the database has no work to do. REQUIRES_NEW makes it worse by holding two connections per thread. With 20 connections and a 3-second partner API call, maximum throughput is only 7 transfers per second. At any higher rate, the pool exhausts and the application fails even though the database is perfectly healthy.

In Rajesh's cross-border transfer service at the National Bank of India, the correct refactor replaces the synchronous REST call inside the transaction with a Transactional Outbox pattern. The transaction contains only database operations: save the transfer and write an outbox event in the same transaction. The connection is held for 10 milliseconds of actual DB work, then released. A separate outbox relay process publishes the event to Kafka, and a partner integration consumer makes the slow REST call with its own connection. Throughput jumps from 7 to 2000 transfers per second because connections are held for milliseconds of actual database work instead of seconds of network waiting.

Pankaj, the architect, enforces a simple rule: transactions must contain only database operations. Network calls, file I/O, and external API calls must happen outside the transaction boundary, either through AFTER_COMMIT event listeners or through the Transactional Outbox pattern with async relay.

Remember one sentence: never hold a database connection while waiting on a network call -- use the Transactional Outbox pattern to keep transactions short and move slow work outside.
